column2: A weaver who plays Pyramus, is "translated" when Puck fixes an ass's nole on his head, becomes the object of Titania's charmed love, and later wants a ballad of the night called "Bottom's Dream."
The carpenter who directs the mechanicals' rehearsal, corrects Bottom's "odious" to "odorous" and Flute's "Ninny's tomb" to "Ninus' tomb," and later calls Bottom "a very paramour for a sweet voice."
The bellows-mender who plays Thisbe, speaks all his part at once including the cue "Ninny's tomb," and later says no man in Athens can discharge Pyramus but Bottom.
The joiner who will play the lion and, in rehearsal planning, is told to show half his face and name himself so the ladies will not be afeard.
The tinker who, seeing Bottom changed, asks what he sees on him, and who is later assigned to present Wall.
The tailor in the mechanicals' company who fears the lion and later reports that Bottom cannot be heard of and is "transported."
Oberon's mischievous sprite who transforms Bottom, anoints the wrong Athenian, says "Lord, what fools these mortals be!," then leads the dueling men astray and remedies Lysander's eyes.
King of the fairies who discovers Puck's mistake, charms Demetrius to love Helena, takes the changeling boy from the still-charmed Titania, and releases her with Dian's bud.
Queen of the fairies who wakes, loves Bottom as an ass, gives Oberon the changeling boy, and after Dian's bud loathes Bottom's visage and is "new in amity" with Oberon.
The four fairies Titania orders to feed, fan, and wait upon Bottom, whom he greets by name with jokes about cobwebs on cuts and mustard that makes eyes water.

The Athenian who, still under the misapplied love-juice, woos Helena, insults Hermia as a "dwarf" and "tawny Tartar," tries to duel Demetrius, and after Puck's remedy wakes again as Hermia's true love.

The Athenian who still pursues Hermia at the start of Act 3, Scene 2, until Oberon charms his eyes, after which he vows love to Helena and later tells Theseus he was betrothed to her before he saw Hermia.

The Athenian woman who loves Demetrius, takes both men's sudden vows as mockery, recalls her "double cherry" friendship with Hermia, and admits she told Demetrius of the lovers' stealth into the wood.
The strong-willed woman who fears Demetrius has slain Lysander, then rages at Helena as a "painted maypole" and "thief of love" when Lysander rejects her.
Duke of Athens who, finding the four lovers asleep after May Day rites, overbears Egeus's will and orders that the three couples be "eternally be knit" in the temple.
Queen of the Amazons and Theseus's bride-to-be, who recalls hunting with Hercules and Cadmus and then leaves with Theseus for the wedding feast.
Hermia's father who, finding her with Lysander, again begs "the law, the law, upon his head," until Theseus overrules him.
Helena's father, who has no speaking part; Egeus identifies the sleeping Helena as "old Nedar's Helena."
